750.title: Rahula the novice
750.hook: the boy sets out water for his father's feet, and the Buddha teaches him with the little water left in the vessel (MN 61)
750.howItsDone: The teaching to Rahula at Ambalatthika (Majjhima Nikaya 61) is taught to novices and children in some Theravada communities as a first lesson in truthfulness and in reflecting before, during and after an action.

segments.voice: Yesterday: appiccha. Anuruddha thought seven thoughts alone in a grove, and the Buddha added the eighth. Your line was few wants. Today, a boy among the great disciples.

Rahula, the Buddha's son, is a novice now, a young monk in training, and tradition says he's about seven. He's staying at a place called Ambalatthika. Toward evening he sees his father coming, and does what a good novice does: he sets out a seat, and water for washing the feet. The Buddha sits, washes his feet, and leaves a little water in the vessel. That little water is the whole lesson plan. Rahula, he asks, do you see this little bit of water left over? Yes, sir.
screen: `A NOVICE SETS OUT WATER.` → `A LITTLE IS LEFT.` → `DO YOU SEE THIS?`

segments.voice: First, the little left over. So little, the Buddha says, is the monk's life of one who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie. It's a stark sentence for a child. But look at what carries it: water Rahula fetched himself, minutes ago, with his own hands. Second, the vessel moves. The Buddha throws the water away. Do you see? Yes, sir. Just so thrown away is the monk's life of one who lies without shame. He turns the vessel upside down: just so overturned. Then upright again, empty: do you see how empty and hollow it is? Just so empty. Picture after picture, all made with one small thing, each a question Rahula can answer. Third, the method. The Buddha never asks Rahula to agree with an idea. He asks him to look. Do you see? And the boy says yes each time, because he does see. The teaching goes into his eyes before his memory. From here the same discourse moves on to an elephant and to a mirror, which we met last year. But it starts with the ladle. Fourth, why a child is taught this way. Truthfulness can sound like a rule from above. Here it's a vessel in a boy's hands: something full or empty, kept or thrown out, an image that could come back whenever he poured water. Gentle, not because the words are soft, but because the lesson is something he can hold.

Turn it over in your mind, the way the Buddha turned the vessel; if no child comes to mind, do it for yourself.

751.title: A handful of sand
751.hook: a commentary story: each morning Rahula took up a handful of sand and wished for as much advice as there were grains in his hand
751.howItsDone: Rahula is remembered in Theravada teaching as the model of a student eager to train, and the handful-of-sand story is told to novices and lay students as a picture of welcoming correction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: musavada. The Buddha taught his young son with the little water left in a vessel. Your line was the ladle of water. Today, what Rahula did with his mornings.

There's a sentence that can make a stomach drop: can I give you some feedback? Rahula, the commentaries say, went looking for it. Every morning, the story goes, he stepped out of his dwelling, bent down, and scooped up a handful of sand. Then he made a wish over it: may I receive today, from the Blessed One and from my teachers, as much advice as there are grains of sand in my hand. Not as much praise. Not as much comfort. As much advice. A boy who asks to be corrected, every day, by the handful.
screen: `A DREADED QUESTION.` → `A HANDFUL EACH MORNING.` → `AS MUCH ADVICE AS THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the list he's on. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha names disciples who stand out, each for one quality, and Rahula is foremost among those who love the training. Not the wisest, not the strongest: the one who most wants to learn. The handful of sand is the commentary's way of showing what that looks like on an ordinary morning. Second, why it's harder than it sounds. Advice means someone has noticed what you're doing wrong. It's easy to want the teaching and skip the correction. Rahula treats correction as something to be gathered, like alms, like water. Third, living close to a teacher. In a short discourse in the Sutta Nipata, the Buddha asks Rahula: does living with a wise man all the time make you look down on him? It's a real danger; familiarity can make a teacher ordinary, and their advice easy to wave away. Rahula says no, he honors the one who holds up the torch for people. The sand is that answer, lived out every morning. Fourth, what it asks of an ordinary day. Nobody could actually receive that much advice in a day, and the story knows it. The point isn't the number. It's the open hand. Last year we heard how his learning ended, with full awakening. The commentaries say this is how it went, day by day: with sand.

752.title: Stubborn Channa
752.hook: the old charioteer is hard to admonish; the Buddha's last instruction is that the community leave him to himself, and the silence turns him (DN 16; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
752.howItsDone: Theravada teachers tell Channa's story as an example of how a community's restraint, rather than punishment, can leave room for a proud person to change, and of how hard it can be to accept advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sikkhakama. Rahula scooped up sand each morning and wished for that much advice. Your line was as much as sand. Today, a monk who wanted none at all.

Back in year one, on the night the prince left the palace, one man was awake with him: Channa, his charioteer, who saddled the horse Kanthaka and rode out beside him. Years later Channa becomes a monk, and that's where the trouble starts. The commentaries say he couldn't forget whose friend he'd been first. It was our Buddha, our teaching, he'd say, and he brushed off the elders who tried to correct him. Then the Buddha is dying, and among the last things he tells Ananda is what should be done about Channa.
screen: `THE CHARIOTEER WHO RODE OUT WITH HIM.` → `A MONK WHO WON'T BE TOLD.` → `A LAST WORD ABOUT CHANNA.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the Mahaparinibbana discourse, the Buddha tells Ananda that after he has gone, Channa should receive the higher penalty, the brahmadanda. What is it, Ananda asks. Let Channa say whatever he likes, the Buddha says, but the monks should neither speak to him, nor advise him, nor instruct him. No expulsion, no scolding: the people he kept brushing off will simply stop trying. Second, the news. The Vinaya tells what happened after the council. Ananda travels to Kosambi, where Channa is living, and tells him. And Channa, hearing that the community will no longer speak to him, falls down in a faint. The proud man, it turns out, cared very much. Third, the turn. Troubled and ashamed, the text says, he goes off to live alone, earnest, diligent, resolute, and before long he reaches the goal the whole path points to. The man who wouldn't accept a word of advice finds the way himself, once nobody is pushing. Fourth, the lifting. Channa asks Ananda to lift the penalty, and Ananda answers that it was lifted already, the moment he was freed. The silence was never meant to outlast the stubbornness; it was the space he needed to soften. The story doesn't make Channa a villain. It makes him the proof: if the charioteer who argued with everyone can wake up, the story suggests, no stubbornness is out of reach. That closes our days with Upali, Anuruddha, Rahula and Channa.

753.title: The first nun
753.hook: Mahapajapati, who raised the Buddha, opens the way for women to go forth, then asks him for a short teaching she can take away and practice (Vinaya, Cullavagga 10; AN 8.53)
753.howItsDone: Mahapajapati Gotami is honored in Buddhist traditions as the founder of the order of nuns, and her brief teaching's eight tests are taught as a way to recognize the Dhamma in any instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: stubborn Channa, left to himself until the silence turned him. Your line was even Channa. Today a new part begins: the women of the order, starting with the one who went first.

She has already done the hard part. In our first year we watched Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha after his mother died, walk to Vesali with the Sakyan women, feet swollen, covered in dust, to ask that women be allowed to go forth. We heard Ananda speak for her, and the answer finally become yes. In the Vinaya, she is the first woman to receive ordination. So what does someone do after she's changed everything? Mahapajapati goes back to her teacher, and asks him for something small.
screen: `THE LONG WALK, IN YEAR ONE.` → `THE DOOR OPENS.` → `AND THEN?`

segments.voice: First, her request. In the Anguttara Nikaya, Mahapajapati asks the Buddha for a teaching in brief, so that she can go off alone and practice it, diligent and resolute. Not a title, not a place of honor: a short teaching she can carry. Second, the answer is a test. Gotami, he says, using her clan name, whatever things you know lead to dispassion, not passion; to release, not bondage; to letting go, not piling up; to few wants, not many; to contentment, not discontent; to solitude, not company; to energy, not laziness; to being easy to support, not burdensome: know for certain that this is the teaching, this is the discipline. Eight tests, each with its opposite. He doesn't hand her a list of beliefs; he hands her a way to check anything. A tool, not a fence. And few wants and contentment may sound familiar from Anuruddha's grove four days ago. Third, her title. The same Anguttara list of outstanding disciples names her foremost among the nuns of long standing, the senior one. She went first, and she stayed. Fourth, her own words. Her verses survive in the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns. In them she gives thanks to the Buddha, and says that through him she was freed from much suffering. The woman who raised him calls him the one who set her free.

754.title: Yasodhara's path
754.hook: the oldest rules call her only Rahula's mother; the commentaries remember her as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great insight (AN 1)
754.howItsDone: In Theravada tradition Yasodhara is remembered through the commentaries and the Apadana as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, and some communities tell her story on its own terms, as a disciple who reached awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhikkhuni. Mahapajapati, the first nun, asked for a teaching she could carry, and got eight tests. Your line was she went first. Today, another woman from the same palace.

A name can disappear inside a relationship. In the Vinaya, when a small boy is sent to ask his father for his inheritance, the woman who sends him isn't called by her name. She's Rahulamata: Rahula's mother. In year one we met her as Yasodhara, the wife the prince left sleeping, and we said her story doesn't end there. In those early pages she stands between two men: the husband who left, the son who followed him. So what happens when the tradition tells her story as her own?
screen: `RAHULA'S MOTHER.` → `THE WIFE LEFT SLEEPING.` → `WHOSE STORY IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, what the old rules give her. In the Vinaya she appears without her name, as Rahula's mother, sending her son out to his father. It's a small part, and it leaves most of her life out. Second, a nun's name. The commentaries say that Yasodhara, too, went forth, after Mahapajapati opened the way, and that as a nun she was known as Bhadda Kaccana. The name Yasodhara belongs to the palace. Bhadda Kaccana belongs to the path. Third, a title of her own. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha names the nun Bhadda Kaccana foremost among those of great higher knowledge. Read with the commentaries, that's Yasodhara, and the honor isn't for being a wife or a mother. It's for what she herself came to see, the same way Upali, Rahula and Mahapajapati were named: for her own quality. Fourth, a farewell. A later collection of verses, the Apadana, gives her a voice at the end of her life. She goes to the Buddha to take her leave, and speaks of her long path in her own words, as one who has arrived. It reads like a later text, full of wonders. But its point is plain. The woman once named only by her son is given her own last word. Her awakening isn't a footnote to his.

755.title: Khema's mirror
755.hook: a commentary story: the proud queen Khema is shown a beautiful woman growing old before her eyes, and understands (Dhammapada 347 story)
755.howItsDone: Khema's story is told with Dhammapada verse 347 in Theravada teaching, and reflection on the body's aging is a traditional practice for loosening attachment, taught with care not to turn it into self-dislike.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yasodhara's path, from Rahula's mother to a nun of great knowledge. Your line was her own awakening. Today, a queen who stayed away.

Some people avoid the doctor because of what the doctor might say. Queen Khema avoided the Buddha for the same reason. She was the chief queen of King Bimbisara, the Dhammapada commentary says, very beautiful, and very proud of it. She had heard that the Buddha spoke about the faults of the body's beauty, and she didn't want to hear it. So the king found a gentle way. He had songs made about the loveliness of the Bamboo Grove, the park where the Buddha stayed, until she wanted to see it for herself. She went to see the gardens. And at the end of the path, there he was.
screen: `A QUEEN WHO STAYED AWAY.` → `SONGS ABOUT A GARDEN.` → `AT THE END OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: First, the vision. The commentary says that as Khema approached, the Buddha caused her to see a young woman standing beside him, fanning him, more beautiful than Khema herself. And Khema thought: next to her, I'm nothing. Second, the change. As she watches, the young woman grows older: youth into middle age, middle age into old age, gray hair, broken teeth, wrinkled skin. Then she falls, and lies still. What takes a lifetime takes moments. This is Khema's mirror: not glass, but a face she envied, showing her what every face will do, her own included. Third, the verse. The commentary places Dhammapada verse three hundred forty-seven here. In Max Muller's old translation it says that those who are slaves to passions run down with the stream, "as a spider runs down the web which he has made himself." Notice where the trouble is. Beauty isn't the enemy in this story. The web is the clinging, and she spun it herself. Fourth, what she did with it. The commentary says Khema understood right there, still wearing her royal ornaments, and with the king's blessing she went forth as a nun. The Anguttara Nikaya names Khema foremost among the nuns in wisdom. The queen who stayed away so she wouldn't hear about aging became a nun remembered for her wisdom.
screen: `A WOMAN MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN HER.` · `A LIFETIME PASSES IN MOMENTS.` · `A WEB YOU SPIN YOURSELF.` · `FOREMOST IN WISDOM.` · then, large: `BEAUTY AGES.`

segments.voice: Use a mirror or a phone camera if one is nearby, or picture your face in your mind, and look at it the way you'd look at someone you love who is getting older: a line by the eyes, a gray hair, or the place where one will be. Don't judge it, and don't fix it; just notice it's changing, as Khema saw, and let the looking stay warm. Then close your eyes, and rest with the breath.
Khema's mirror. A vision of a beautiful woman growing old, which showed a proud queen the web she'd spun herself. Today's word.
Your line: beauty ages. She saw it, and was free of the web. Rest well.

756.title: Khema answers the king
756.hook: King Pasenadi asks the nun Khema whether the Tathagata exists after death; she answers with the sand of the Ganges and the depth of the ocean, and later the Buddha answers the same (SN 44.1)
756.howItsDone: Khema's conversation with King Pasenadi is studied in Theravada teaching on the undeclared questions, and is told as an example of a nun whose understanding matched the Buddha's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khema's mirror. A proud queen saw beauty age in moments and walked out of the web. Your line was beauty ages. Today, Khema the nun, and a king with a hard question.

A king on the road, with a night to fill. In the Samyutta Nikaya, King Pasenadi of Kosala is traveling between two cities and stops for the night at a small town. He sends a man to find an ascetic or a brahmin worth talking to. The man finds none. Only the nun Khema, a disciple of the Buddha, whom people describe as wise, learned, and a brilliant speaker. So the king goes to her, bows, sits to one side, and asks: when a fully awakened one dies, what happens to him? Does he exist after death?
screen: `A KING ON THE ROAD.` → `ONLY ONE TEACHER IN TOWN.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER DEATH?`

segments.voice: First, four questions, one answer. Does the Tathagata, the one thus gone, exist after death? That hasn't been declared by the Blessed One, great king, Khema says. Then he doesn't exist? Not declared. Both? Neither? Not declared, each time. The king, puzzled, asks why. Second, the sand and the sea. Khema answers with a question. Great king, do you have an accountant who could count the grains of sand in the Ganges? No. Could anyone measure the water in the great ocean? No; it's deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom. Just so, Khema says. The awakened one has let go of the body, the feelings and the rest, all the things we'd use to measure him. Freed from that reckoning, he is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom, like the ocean. Third, the second conversation. Later the king asks the Buddha himself the same four questions. The Buddha gives the same answers and the same similes, and the king says it's wonderful how teacher and disciple agree, in meaning and in wording. Fourth, a teacher in her own right. Khema claimed nothing of her own: not declared by the Blessed One, she said, each time. She had understood it herself, so well that his words and hers matched. And notice the sand. A few days ago Rahula held a handful each morning, wishing for advice. Khema holds a whole river's worth, and uses it to say: some things can't be counted.
screen: `NOT DECLARED, EACH TIME.` · `SAND IN THE GANGES, WATER IN THE SEA.` · `THE TEACHER SAYS THE SAME.` · `SHE SAW IT HERSELF.` · then, large: `THE SAME ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something without a title, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend who simply understood, and recall one thing they said that turned out to be true. Then let the big questions you carry stay unanswered for a minute, without counting or measuring them. Just breathe, deep and hard to fathom, like the ocean in Khema's answer.
Abyakata, undeclared. The questions the Buddha set aside, which Khema answered King Pasenadi the same way, with the simile of the ocean. Today's word.
Your line: the same answer. Not repeating him, but seeing the same thing. Day seven hundred fifty-six.
